title: Living Food: The Science of Fermentation
context:
People have been fermenting food for at least nine thousand years. Chemical traces in pottery from northern China show that Neolithic villagers made a drink from rice, honey and fruit, and later civilisations discovered that milk, grain, fish and vegetables could all be transformed in a similar way. Their motive was probably practical rather than culinary. In a world without refrigerators, fermentation allowed a seasonal harvest to be stored for months. Many of these foods are still central to national cuisines, from yoghurt in the Balkans to kimchi in Korea.

The process is carried out by microorganisms, mostly bacteria, yeasts and moulds, which feed on sugars and release acids, alcohol or gases. Consider sauerkraut. When cabbage is shredded and mixed with salt, water is drawn out of the leaves, creating a brine. Harmful microbes struggle in this salty liquid, while lactic acid bacteria, which are already present on the leaves, multiply. As they feed they produce lactic acid, and once the acidity reaches a certain level few dangerous organisms can survive. This explains why many traditional ferments are safe, although it would be wrong to suppose that all of them are. Badly controlled fermentation of some meats and fish has caused serious poisoning.

Preservation is only part of the story. Microbes also alter flavour and nutrition. They break down proteins into amino acids, among them glutamate, which gives soy sauce, miso and aged cheese their savoury depth. Some ferments contain additional vitamins, and in cereal doughs the activity of microbes reduces phytic acid, a compound that prevents the body from absorbing minerals such as iron and zinc. Sourdough bread is sometimes said to be more nutritious than ordinary bread for this reason, though the effect depends heavily on how long the dough is left to rise.

Health claims for fermented foods are more contentious. Supporters point to probiotics, live bacteria that may benefit the gut. In one trial, volunteers who added fermented foods to their diet for ten weeks showed a greater variety of gut bacteria and lower levels of chemical markers of inflammation than a group who ate more fibre. The study was small, however, and independent scientists urge caution. Many shop-bought products are heat-treated before sale, which kills the organisms that supposedly provide the benefit, and some researchers suspect that the compounds produced during fermentation, rather than the living microbes, may be responsible for any improvement.

A different debate concerns the way fermentation is done. Large manufacturers use carefully selected starter cultures to guarantee speed, safety and a consistent taste. Artisans reply that relying on wild microbes gives richer, more varied flavours. It is often assumed that those microbes come from the region, so that bread from one city will always taste different from bread from another. A worldwide survey of sourdough starters, however, found that geography explained very little. Factors such as the type of flour and the hands of the baker proved to be more important.

Whatever the truth of the individual claims, interest in fermentation shows no sign of fading. Home cooks fill jars with cabbage and carrots, and restaurants list their own house-made vinegars. The enthusiasm is understandable, since few cooking techniques are so cheap or so rewarding. Yet a little scepticism is healthy. Fermentation is a craft with a long history, not a miracle cure, and the evidence for its benefits should be judged by the same standards as any other medical claim.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about the earliest fermentation?
options: It was invented to produce alcohol
It was practised only in China
It began with the discovery of lactic acid
It was probably used mainly to store food
questions.answer: It was probably used mainly to store food
questions.why: Động cơ có lẽ thực dụng hơn là ẩm thực: cho phép trữ mùa thu hoạch nhiều tháng.
questions.quote: Their motive was probably practical rather than culinary.

questions.prompt: What do the chemical traces in the Chinese pottery show?
options: Villagers stored milk in clay jars
Villagers produced a drink from rice, honey and fruit
Villagers traded fermented fish
Villagers baked bread from grain
questions.answer: Villagers produced a drink from rice, honey and fruit
questions.why: Dấu vết hoá học cho thấy cư dân Tân thạch làm đồ uống từ gạo, mật ong, trái cây.
questions.quote: made a drink from rice, honey and fruit

questions.prompt: Why is salt important in making sauerkraut?
options: It draws water from the leaves and makes conditions hard for harmful microbes
It kills the bacteria that cause cabbage to spoil
It provides the sugars that microbes feed on
It prevents any acid from forming
questions.answer: It draws water from the leaves and makes conditions hard for harmful microbes
questions.why: Muối hút nước tạo nước muối, vi khuẩn có hại khó phát triển trong đó.
questions.quote: Harmful microbes struggle in this salty liquid

questions.prompt: Where do the lactic acid bacteria in sauerkraut come from?
options: They are added as a starter
They come from the salt
They are already on the cabbage leaves
They are in the water used
questions.answer: They are already on the cabbage leaves
questions.why: Vi khuẩn lactic có sẵn trên lá bắp cải.
questions.quote: which are already present on the leaves

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the safety of fermented foods?
options: All traditional ferments are safe
Acidity makes every ferment dangerous
Fish ferments are always safer than meat ones
Acidity explains why many ferments are safe, but not all are
questions.answer: Acidity explains why many ferments are safe, but not all are
questions.why: Độ axit giải thích vì sao nhiều món lên men an toàn, nhưng một số thịt, cá lên men kém kiểm soát từng gây ngộ độc.
questions.quote: it would be wrong to suppose that all of them are

questions.prompt: What is the role of glutamate?
options: It gives savoury depth to foods such as soy sauce and miso
It helps to preserve foods for longer
It increases the vitamin content of dough
It prevents minerals from being absorbed
questions.answer: It gives savoury depth to foods such as soy sauce and miso
questions.why: Glutamate tạo vị đậm đà (umami) cho tương, miso, phô mai.
questions.quote: gives soy sauce, miso and aged cheese their savoury depth

questions.prompt: What is the effect of reducing phytic acid in dough?
options: The bread rises faster
The bread contains less sugar
The body can absorb more minerals
The bread tastes more sour
questions.answer: The body can absorb more minerals
questions.why: Phytic acid cản trở hấp thu khoáng như sắt, kẽm; giảm nó giúp hấp thu tốt hơn.
questions.quote: prevents the body from absorbing minerals such as iron and zinc

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about sourdough bread?
options: It is always more nutritious than ordinary bread
Its advantage depends on how long the dough rises
It is less nutritious when the dough is left to rise
Its benefits have been proved in trials
questions.answer: Its advantage depends on how long the dough rises
questions.why: Hiệu quả phụ thuộc nhiều vào thời gian ủ bột.

easy to prove
rarely discussed
likely to cause disagreement

Wild ferments are quicker
